But some banks raised "substantial amounts of new capital." Q3 GDP revised up sharply (inventory-led) but Q4 "decelerated significantly." Consumer spending "nearly flat" in Sep-Oct. Housing correction "deeper and more prolonged." Equipment orders "declined" in October. Staff: GDP "noticeably below potential in 2008." Statement: Dropped explicit risk balance again — "heightened uncertainty." "Economic growth is slowing." Dollar appreciated this period. "Risk of an unfavorable feedback loop" discussed. UE 4.7%.

DRUG TESTING JOKE — Stockton: "forecast could admittedly be described as a pretty rosy picture" — achieved "modest edging-off of inflation" despite turmoil — "I was worried personally when I received a notice the other day that the Board would begin frequent drug-testing for certain members of the staff"; assures projection made "unimpaired and on our own — fueled only by countless late nights of diet Pepsi and vending-machine Twinkies." GDP FLAT IN Q4 — "remarkable deceleration" from 5% in Q3 to flat in Q4; "considerable darkening of our outlook"; 2008 at 1¼%. MUDDLE-THROUGH AS AVERAGE OF TWO EXTREMES — "muddle-through scenario is increasingly looking like the average of two considerably less benign outcomes" — resilient bounce-back with more inflation vs "drop below stall speed and the economy experiences outright recession." Stockton: "I would readily acknowledge those risks" but still sees muddle-through as "more plausible." MARCH 1999 VS FALL 2000 — Revisited both analogies from September: 1998 parallel (overestimated restraint) seems "less likely to me now" because data "lining up comfortably with our projection of slower growth." 2000 parallel (missed recession) "can't be ruled out" but "noteworthy differences" — no "grim stories" from manufacturers yet about "dismal state of order books." ANOMALY_NOTE: MONETARY POLICY FRAMEWORK REVIEW — THIRD INSTALLMENT (TOOLS) — Two staff presentations on monetary policy tools. Key elements: (1) FORWARD GUIDANCE (Zarutskie) — Three variants: qualitative (vague, flexible), date-based (specific date), outcome-based (tied to macro outcomes); "strong case that date-based and outcome-based forward guidance" more effective than qualitative; "Delphic" risk — guidance may be "misinterpreted as conveying news about a deteriorating economic outlook"; SEP can "help support and reinforce" forward guidance; escape clauses "add complexity" but provide "flexibility." (2) FORWARD GUIDANCE AWAY FROM ELB — "Limited empirical evidence" but "a few studies have shown that such forward guidance could be effective in altering expectations about the future course of policy"; could reinforce commitment to inflation target. (3) NEGATIVE INTEREST RATE POLICY — No central bank below -1%; "appears that such policies have eased financial conditions and supported economic activity, on balance"; but adverse bank profitability effects, deposit tiering needed; U.S. challenges: money market fund role much larger; "host of operational changes both within the Federal Reserve and in the larger financial system" needed. (4) BALANCE SHEET TOOLS (D'Amico) — QE evidence: "significant pass-through to prices of higher-quality private assets" and "modestly higher inflation"; "marginal benefits of QE programs did not diminish"; but duration-risk channel "might be weakened" at very low long-term rates. (5) FLOW-BASED VS FIXED-SIZE QE — Flow-based (like QE3) has "automatic stabilizing function"; aligning with forward guidance "attenuates risk of two tools working at cross-purposes"; fixed-size "might be preferable in the case of a large, persistent shock." (6) YIELD CURVE CONTROL — Ceilings on short rates: easier to maintain credibility, smaller balance sheet; on longer-term rates: affects rates relevant to households/businesses but "harder to maintain" and "more sensitive to factors other than monetary policy"; "should be particularly effective in reducing investor uncertainty." (7) NON-GOVERNMENT BOND PURCHASES — MBS, credit facilities, "funding for lending"; more targeted but "may create political economy challenges" and increased credit risk.

ANOMALY_NOTE: MONETARY POLICY FRAMEWORK REVIEW — FIFTH INSTALLMENT (INFLATION RANGES AND FINANCIAL STABILITY) — Two staff presentations concluding the pre-COVID framework review. Key elements: (1) INFLATION RANGES (Chung) — Three types: "uncertainty range" (communicates expected variation under appropriate policy), "operational range" (signals Committee prefers inflation temporarily away from target, e.g., 2-2½% after below-target periods), and "indifference range" (no policy response within range, e.g., 1¾-3%); most AFE central banks use uncertainty ranges; operational range could support average inflation targeting by defining scope of acceptable overshoot; indifference range risks expectations drift — simulations show "average level of inflation is only slightly larger than under a standard framework" but expectations could drift. (2) FINANCIAL STABILITY AND MONETARY POLICY (Klee) — Asset valuation elasticities: 100bp rate decline → corporate spreads -20bp, stock market +4-5pp, house prices +2-4pp; "elasticities are modest in magnitude relative to the overall variation" → "changes in monetary policy generally affect valuation pressures by amounts that likely have limited effects on financial stability"; makeup strategy simulations: rates 50bp lower for many years; model implies asset price changes "would be modest, given the estimated elasticities" but rules out "outsized asset price responses that have sometimes characterized episodes of financial instability." (3) TOOLS AND FINANCIAL STABILITY — Forward guidance: "reach for yield" risk, leverage buildup if markets certain policy on hold; QE: disproportionate longer-term borrowing encouragement, yield curve flattening disrupting business models, "some indication that QE leads to reach-for-yield behavior"; overall: "little evidence that unconventional monetary policy contributed significantly to financial vulnerabilities" but "past experience is limited, particularly with respect to times when the economy is at or close to full employment." (4) MACROPRUDENTIAL LIMITATIONS — U.S. toolkit "somewhat limited" vs other countries; "generally only affect banks"; no borrower-based tools (LTV ratios); require interagency coordination. (5) LAST PRE-COVID FRAMEWORK SESSION — This was the final framework review installment before COVID-19 disrupted the review process; Committee was approaching deliberation phase on revised consensus statement.
